reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Phantom limb pain is painful sensation perceived in a limb or body part that has been amputated, and must be distinguished from non-painful phantom sensation and from residual limb (stump) pain
Most amputees experience some phantom phenomena; pain often begins within the first days to weeks after amputation and may follow a telescoping pattern where the phantom seems to shorten over time
Pre-amputation limb pain and its intensity are recognised risk factors, and the phantom pain may echo the character of the pain felt before surgery
Careful examination of the residual limb is essential to separate phantom pain from stump pain caused by neuroma, poor prosthetic fit, infection, or ischaemia
Non-pharmacological approaches including mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, desensitisation, and early prosthetic use address the cortical reorganisation thought to drive the pain
Pharmacological principles favour neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids and certain antidepressants, with opioids reserved and used cautiously
A multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach that combines prosthetic training, psychological support, and pain management gives the best functional outcomes
Perioperative and preventive analgesic strategies may reduce the likelihood or severity of later phantom pain
reference.pathophysiology: Phantom limb pain arises from maladaptive changes at multiple levels of the nervous system after amputation. Peripherally, injured axons form neuromas that generate ectopic and spontaneous discharge. In the spinal cord, deafferentation leads to central sensitisation and disinhibition of dorsal horn neurons. Within the brain, the somatosensory and motor cortices undergo reorganisation, with cortical territory representing the missing limb being invaded by adjacent regions; the degree of this remapping correlates with pain intensity. Psychological factors and pre-existing pain memory further modulate the experience.
additionalDifferentials: Prosthetic-related mechanical pain or pressure injury
Residual limb infection or wound breakdown
Referred pain from the spine or proximal joints
Heterotopic ossification in the residual limb
additionalInvestigations: Clinical history and examination distinguishing phantom pain from stump pain and non-painful phantom sensation
Inspection and palpation of the residual limb for neuroma, tenderness, and prosthetic fit
Imaging of the residual limb where neuroma, heterotopic ossification, or bony spur is suspected
Vascular assessment if ischaemia of the residual limb is a concern
Assessment for infection when there are local inflammatory signs or wound problems
redFlags: Residual limb signs of infection or wound dehiscence requiring urgent treatment
Features of critical ischaemia in the residual limb
Rapidly worsening or new pain pattern suggesting an alternative surgical or vascular cause
Severe intractable pain with mood deterioration and suicidal ideation
reference.prognosis: Phantom pain often diminishes in frequency and intensity over the months to years following amputation, and many patients cope well with a combination of therapy and prosthetic use. A subset develop persistent, treatment-resistant pain that requires ongoing multidisciplinary management.
pitfalls: Confusing phantom pain with stump pain and missing a treatable neuroma or prosthetic-fit problem
Neglecting early prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation, which can worsen cortical reorganisation
Dismissing patient reports of pain in an absent limb as psychological
Over-reliance on opioids for a fundamentally neuropathic pain problem
Overlooking pre-amputation pain control that could reduce later phantom pain
management: Non-pharmacological cortical retraining with mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, desensitisation and early prosthetic use to counter maladaptive cortical reorganisation
Neuropathic pharmacotherapy with gabapentinoids and antidepressants such as tricyclics or SNRIs, with opioids reserved and used cautiously
Optimisation of the residual limb and prosthetic fit, with treatment of stump pathology such as neuroma, poor fit, infection or ischaemia that mimics or aggravates the pain
Perioperative and preventive analgesia around amputation, addressing pre-amputation pain as a recognised risk factor
Interventional options for refractory pain including nerve blocks, targeted muscle reinnervation and neuromodulation or spinal cord stimulation
Psychological support such as cognitive behavioural therapy for the affective component and pain-related distress
Coordinated rehabilitation medicine and pain-team care for persistent, treatment-resistant pain
